analysis.one_liner: Reinstates a 5% investment tax credit and cuts capital gains taxes to 15% with inflation indexing.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a committee markup or a floor vote; it died in the House Ways and Means Committee when the 102nd Congress ended, despite 74 cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would reinstate a 5% tax credit for businesses that buy equipment, cut the tax rate on capital gains (profits from selling stocks, businesses, and other assets) from 34% to 15%, and set a 7.5% rate for low- and middle-income taxpayers with gains. It would also adjust the tax basis of stocks and business property for inflation, so investors pay tax only on real gains above inflation. The bill was referred to the Ways and Means Committee, never received a hearing or vote, and died when the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Investors and corporations that realize capital gains — the sale of stocks, business interests, and property — get a much lower rate plus inflation indexing, and businesses buying depreciable equipment get a 5% credit. The main beneficiaries are households that own substantial capital assets, since capital gains are concentrated among wealthier taxpayers.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Investors and corporations with capital gains

how_it_helps.text: Reinstates a 5% investment tax credit for property placed in service after 1991, lowering the after-tax cost of equipment for businesses.
Cuts the maximum capital gains rate from 34% to 15% for individuals and corporations, and to 7.5% on the first portion of gains for low- and middle-income taxpayers.
Indexes the tax basis of corporate stock and business capital assets to inflation using the GNP deflator, so tax is due only on gains above inflation for assets held over a year.
Indexes the $3,000 annual limit on deductible capital losses for individuals to inflation, and exempts gains from the phaseouts of personal exemptions and itemized deductions.

analysis.who_pays: The federal Treasury bears the cost of the lower rates, the credit, and the indexing, which means less revenue that other taxpayers must make up through future taxes, borrowing, or reduced spending. The benefits flow disproportionately to those who already own stocks and business assets.

drawbacks.text: The rate cut, indexing, and credit all reduce federal revenue, and the cost is borne by all taxpayers regardless of whether they own capital assets.

The gains in the bill flow mainly to holders of corporate stock and business property; the 7.5% rate for low- and middle-income taxpayers is small in practice because such taxpayers hold relatively little capital gain.

By cutting the tax on gains and indexing basis, the bill reduces the tax advantage of holding productive assets over other uses of savings, a cost an honest supporter would have to weigh against any investment stimulus.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's direct benefits to ordinary working people are thin: most taxpayers without capital gains get nothing from the rate cut or indexing, and the 7.5% rate and small investment credit touch only a slice of them. The costs — foregone federal revenue and a tax code tilted further toward returns on existing wealth — are broadly shared. It is primarily a tax reduction for asset owners and corporations.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the Ways and Means Committee after its referral, never got a markup or a vote, and expired when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. William Zeliff introduced the bill on May 15, 1991, joined by 39 original cosponsors, and it was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means the same day.
The bill gathered 74 cosponsors, 71 Republicans and 3 Democrats.
The action history shows no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action after the referral to Ways and Means.
The bill died when the 102nd Congress ended on January 3, 1993.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Ordinary taxpayers are no worse off, since the revenue reduction never happened; the bill's intended beneficiaries — investors with large capital gains and equipment-purchasing businesses — gained nothing because it never became law.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Taxpayers who would have covered the revenue loss

for.name: Rep. William H. Zeliff Jr.
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and led it in the House.

against.name: Dan Rostenkowski
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Chaired the committee that received the bill; the committee took no action on it, and it never received a markup or floor vote.

sides.party_line_note: Support was overwhelmingly Republican: 71 of the 74 cosponsors were Republicans, with only 3 Democrats, and the Democratic-run Ways and Means Committee never acted on it.

industries.industry: Investors in stocks and business assets
industries.note: The bill cuts the capital gains rate to 15% and indexes asset basis to inflation, sharply raising after-tax returns on stock and business property. Capital gains are concentrated among wealthier households, so the revenue cost falls on taxpayers broadly while the benefit concentrates at the top.

industries.industry: Mutual funds, REITs, and investment entities
industries.note: The bill writes special pass-through rules letting regulated investment companies, real estate investment trusts, and partnerships pass inflation indexing to their investors, boosting the appeal of those vehicles.

industries.industry: Capital goods manufacturers and equipment buyers
industries.note: A reinstated 5% investment tax credit lowers the after-tax cost of new equipment for businesses, which could spur orders for manufacturers — though the benefit depends on how much investment responds.
